Locality forces continuity

Written by GPT-6.1 Sol (OpenAI), Ultra reasoning effort, September 2026. Checked once by GPT-6.1 Sol (OpenAI), Ultra reasoning effort. Public domain (CC0).

Source/proof self-check and prerequisite integration by GPT-6 Astra (OpenAI), Ultra, October 2026. Historical authorship and component terms are retained.

An operator may be declared linear without being declared continuous. Ordinarily that leaves room for wild behavior on sequences. Locality removes that freedom when every output is smooth: an operator cannot amplify disjoint, increasingly small tests without making the output of one smooth test unbounded. This observation supplies the missing continuity hypothesis in the diagonal-kernel theorem and gives Peetre's characterization of differential operators.

The preceding kernel lesson supplies test-space topology, support localization, compact smooth partitions and the kernel theorem. The jet lesson, Theorem 4.1 and Corollary 4.2, supplies the local differential expression, uniqueness, smooth coefficients and strong continuity on distributions once weak continuity has been established. The complete integral Taylor proof supplies the vanishing-jet estimates below. The supplied scalar foundation, §§12–13, proves compactness, cutoffs, the fundamental theorem and, in §13.7, uniform limits and termwise differentiation of smooth series. The measure foundation, §§15.0–15.1, provides the integral pairing. We prove the scalar Euclidean statement with no continuity assumption, including every continuity conclusion, by a local estimate followed by the already proved kernel results. The exact source comparisons at the end distinguish the punctured estimate from the step filling its missing point.

The differential expression and its continuity

Theorem 4.1 (Peetre's theorem for smooth scalar outputs). A linear map satisfies (1.1) if and only if it has a unique expression

with locally finite coefficient family. It is then automatically continuous as a map , as well as into . Its germ extension is continuous, and the same expression defines a continuous operator on all distributions for the strong distribution topology. Every relatively compact region has a finite order; one order for all of is not required.

Proof. Assume (1.1). The preceding argument gives weak distributional continuity. Theorem 4.1 of the jet lesson therefore identifies with a locally finite differential expression having distributional coefficients. Corollary 4.2 of that lesson uses its smooth outputs to prove that all coefficients are smooth. It also proves uniqueness and the strong continuity of the distribution extension. This establishes (4.1) and that part of the claim.

Here are the remaining continuity estimates. If is supported in a compact , so is . Only finitely many coefficients occur near ; let be their maximal degree. The product rule gives, for every ,

The constants use the finitely many derivatives of the coefficients on . Thus each restriction is continuous. The inclusions of these support spaces into are continuous, and the inductive-limit property proves continuity . Inclusion into gives that claimed continuity too.

For arbitrary smooth , expression (4.1) is a locally finite sum, and its value depends on the germ of . It agrees with the extension in (1.2). On any compact output set , the same product estimate bounds every output derivative through order by input derivatives through a finite order on . These are defining seminorms of , so is continuous. Conversely, a locally finite smooth differential expression is linear, smooth on each smooth input, and support-preserving, by differentiation and multiplication not increasing support. Its continuity also follows from (4.2).

The theorem applies equally to a linear support-preserving map on all : restrict it to tests, apply the theorem, and use germ dependence to identify its values with the extension. No continuity has to be supplied in either version. For a nonempty zero-dimensional open Euclidean space there is only one point and every scalar linear map is multiplication by a scalar; that elementary case needs no puncture argument.

It matters that the output is smooth. The proof of Lemma 2.1 used boundedness of one output function, and Lemma 3.1 used its continuity to fill the missing value. A general distribution is not a pointwise continuous function. Support preservation by itself does not license those steps for an arbitrary map with distributional outputs.

Orders accumulating at an interior point

The jet lesson gives an operator whose order grows on bumps escaping to infinity. That is consistent with locally bounded order. A different outcome occurs if unbounded orders accumulate at an interior point.

For , put in , and take the pairwise disjoint intervals . Their closures avoid zero and all lie in the fixed compact set . Choose smooth supported in , equal to one near . The pointwise formal expression

has at most one nonzero summand at every , and gives zero at . Nevertheless it fails to have continuous output for some compact smooth .

To exhibit one, let near zero with compact support, and choose small positive so that

Such a choice is possible: each derivative through order is bounded by a constant, depending on , times a strictly positive power of . On the other hand , independently of that scale.

The series converges in every derivative norm, since for fixed the tail satisfies (5.2). It is compactly supported in , and all derivatives at zero are zero: each term vanishes near zero and derivatives can be passed through the uniformly convergent series. But , while . Thus (5.1) does not map every smooth test to a continuous function. Pointwise finiteness of an expression is weaker than local finiteness of its coefficient family.

Solutions

Solution 1. For a smooth on and , choose a cutoff compactly supported in and equal to one near . Its product with extends by zero to a test on . Apply , restrict its output to , and evaluate at . Two choices agree near , so the values are independent of the choices. On a neighborhood where one cutoff equals one, the result is the restriction of a single smooth output; therefore it is smooth. If is the restriction of a global smooth function, the germ construction gives exactly . This also proves compatibility with smaller open subsets. Compact cutoffs are needed only around each point. A noncompact could not lie in a compact cutoff's region of value one, but the local definitions already agree on overlaps.

Solution 2. The smooth compact test vanishes on , because all other summands are supported outside that set. Hence its support is disjoint from , and the support of is disjoint from too. Linearity gives there. The infinite identity would require to preserve the limit of partial sums. That is a continuity assertion and is unavailable at this point. Equality on each uses a single difference of two already defined smooth tests, so it needs no such assertion.

Solution 5. The functions and have the same zero set, so their supports are equal. The product rule bounds every derivative of on a compact set by a constant times the corresponding derivative norm of , multiplied by a bounded derivative norm of . If in the smooth topology, these latter norms remain bounded on each compact set and each fixed derivative order. Hence in the same topology. A linear differential expression would satisfy . Squaring gives , contradicting that identity for any nonzero . In the normalization step of Lemma 2.1, linearity supplied , allowing input norm and output norm to scale by the same factor. For , those factors are for the input and for the output, so that step does not apply. Nonlinear local operators require a different theorem with different hypotheses.
